articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to blocking and rejecting transactions, as well as filing reports with OFAC. This update is part of an ongoing review process to ensure that published guidance remains current and relevant.

The amendments cover FAQs 10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53. These FAQs provide critical guidance for financial institutions and other entities on their obligations under OFAC sanctions programs, particularly concerning the handling of blocked property and rejected transactions, and the proper procedures for submitting required reports to the agency.
The updated guidance aims to clarify compliance expectations and assist U.S. persons in navigating the complexities of sanctions regulations, thereby reducing the risk of inadvertent violations.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related and Russia-Related General Licenses, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and the issuance of Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses. Concurrently, OFAC has removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.

Specifically, OFAC issued Iran General License GG, 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving Karnakis and Karnakis,' and Iran General License HH, 'Authorizing Wind Down Activities, Limited Safety and Environmental Transactions, and the Offloading of Cargo Involving Certain Persons or Vessels Blocked on October 21, 2026.' Additionally, Russia-related General License 131K was issued, authorizing certain transactions for the negotiation and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities.

The action also included the addition of several individuals and vessels to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List under Iran-related authorities, while certain individuals were removed from the SDN list under Belarus and North Korea sanctions programs.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA)
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA), targeting entities involved in activities that undermine American intellectual property.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued PAIPA General License 1, 'Transactions Authorized Pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations,' and PAIPA General License 2, 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving Certain Entities Blocked on October 19, 2026.'

One entity added to OFAC's Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions List is BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN PHASE I VENTURE CAPITAL CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP (a.k.a. MIRACLE PLUS RMB FUND I), located in Beijing, China. The designation includes blocking of property, prohibitions on loans from U.S. financial institutions exceeding $10,000,000 in any 12-month period, and prohibitions on foreign exchange and banking transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This action aims to provide updated guidance and clarity regarding certain transactions involving Venezuela.

The specific details of the amended General License and FAQ were not immediately released, but such updates typically address evolving policy considerations or provide technical corrections to existing authorizations. These amendments are crucial for entities and individuals engaging in authorized activities with Venezuela to ensure ongoing compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.
Stakeholders are advised to review the updated guidance carefully to understand any changes to permissible activities or reporting requirements under the Venezuela sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba-Related Entities, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation, alongside the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs).

Among the Iran-related actions, OFAC issued Iran-related General License FF, 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.' The designations also included individuals such as Azadeh Abdolalipur, linked to Farab Soroush Afagh Qeshm Company, added to the SDN List under Iran-related authorities.

Additionally, a new Cuba-related FAQ (FAQ 1276) was issued, and an existing Russia-related FAQ (FAQ 1225) was amended. The Department of State also designated the Cuban state-owned Banco Internacional de Comercio, S.A. (BICSA).

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation from its sanctions lists. This action signifies a de-escalation of sanctions against a specific entity or individual previously targeted under the Venezuela sanctions program.

Designation removals typically occur when the sanctioned party meets certain criteria, such as demonstrating a change in behavior, no longer posing a threat, or providing information that warrants their delisting. The specific reasons for this particular removal were not immediately detailed.

This development is important for entities monitoring changes in the Venezuela sanctions landscape, as it may impact permissible interactions and due diligence requirements related to the delisted party.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This action aims to disrupt illicit networks that pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

The designations were imposed pursuant to Executive Order 14059, which targets the international proliferation of illicit drugs, and Executive Order 13224, as amended, which targets terrorists and their supporters.

This action is part of ongoing efforts by the U.S. Treasury to combat transnational criminal organizations and terrorist financing, reinforcing the commitment to dismantle networks that facilitate drug trafficking and support terrorism globally.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates International Criminal Court
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a freight forwarding firm, for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. Concurrently, OFAC has designated the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued related General Licenses, while also removing a Burma-related designation.

The designation of the International Criminal Court (ICC) was made pursuant to Executive Order 14203, adding the entire institution to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List).

In parallel, OFAC issued four General Licenses related to the ICC: GL 13, 'Authorizing Certain Transactions Involving the International Criminal Court'; GL 14, 'Authorizing Certain Transactions Related to Telecommunications and Enterprise Software Involving the International Criminal Court'; GL 15, 'Authorizing Transactions Related to Pension Payments Involving the International Criminal Court'; and GL 16, 'Authorizing Certain Transactions Related to Certain International Criminal Court Detainees.'

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Russia-Related General License Authorizing Diesel Fuel Transactions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Russia-related General License 135, 'Authorizing Transactions Related to the Sale, Delivery, Offloading, and Importation of Diesel Fuel of Russian Federation Origin.'

This General License temporarily authorizes certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Russian Harmful Foreign Activities Sanctions Regulations and the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations. The authorization is in effect through April 7, 2027.
The issuance of this license comes amidst rising global diesel prices and follows an announcement by President Trump regarding an agreement with Russia to release diesel fuel to global markets.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 in OFAC Settlement
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., resulting in a civil penalty of $11,662,930. This penalty is part of broader enforcement actions against the bank for violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.
The settlement addresses apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

This OFAC penalty is in addition to significant fines levied by the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) for related BSA/AML deficiencies.

The settlement with the freight forwarding firm was announced alongside other OFAC actions, including the designation of the International Criminal Court.
This enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued focus on ensuring compliance across various industries involved in international trade and logistics.

body: An individual has entered into a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), agreeing to pay a civil penalty of $1,427,230. The details of the apparent violations were not immediately disclosed in the summary.

This enforcement action underscores OFAC's authority to pursue penalties against individuals who violate U.S. sanctions laws, even in cases not involving corporate entities. The specific nature of the violations typically involves unauthorized transactions with sanctioned persons, entities, or jurisdictions.
Such penalties serve as a deterrent and emphasize the importance of individual compliance with OFAC regulations, regardless of professional affiliation.

This penalty serves as a reminder to all businesses, regardless of size or industry, of the importance of adhering to U.S. sanctions laws and regulations.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,050,000
body: FTI Consulting, Inc. has entered into a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), agreeing to pay a civil penalty of $1,050,000. The settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

The nature of the violations typically involves providing services or engaging in transactions that contravene U.S. sanctions programs. Consulting firms, like all U.S. persons, are required to ensure their activities do not directly or indirectly benefit sanctioned parties or jurisdictions.

This enforcement action highlights the need for professional services firms to implement stringent sanctions compliance measures, especially when operating internationally or advising clients with global footprints.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Fined $275,000,000 by OFAC
body: Adani Enterprises Limited has been assessed a significant civil penalty of $275,000,000 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This substantial fine indicates serious apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.

While the specific details of the violations were not immediately provided, penalties of this magnitude often relate to extensive or systemic breaches involving major sanctions programs, such as those targeting proliferators of weapons of mass destruction, state sponsors of terrorism, or significant transactions with sanctioned jurisdictions.

This enforcement action serves as a strong warning to large multinational corporations about the critical importance of comprehensive and effective sanctions compliance programs to prevent engagement in prohibited activities.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Pays $1,110,661 in OFAC Settlement
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc. has entered into a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), agreeing to pay a civil penalty of $1,110,661. The settlement addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

Financial institutions, including brokerage firms, are under strict obligations to screen their customers and transactions against OFAC's sanctions lists and to block or reject prohibited activities. Failures in these compliance controls can lead to significant penalties.
This enforcement action highlights the ongoing vigilance required from financial services providers to prevent sanctioned individuals or entities from accessing the U.S. financial system.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $3,777,000 in OFAC Settlement
body: An individual has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), resulting in a civil penalty of $3,777,000. This substantial fine indicates serious apparent violations of U.S. sanctions laws by an individual.

Individual penalties from OFAC typically stem from direct involvement in prohibited transactions, facilitating sanctions evasion, or engaging with sanctioned parties or jurisdictions. The magnitude of this penalty suggests a significant or willful breach of regulations.
This action serves as a stark reminder that individuals, not just corporations, are subject to OFAC's enforcement authority and can face severe financial consequences for non-compliance.

This enforcement action underscores the broad reach of OFAC's jurisdiction and the necessity for all types of organizations to implement and maintain effective sanctions compliance programs.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026, Including Penalties Against American Express and Bank of America
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has released its enforcement actions for October 2026, targeting several financial institutions and individuals for various violations. These actions are taken to ensure compliance with banking laws and regulations and to address unsafe or unsound practices.

Among the significant actions, the OCC issued a Cease and Desist Order and a Civil Money Penalty against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah, for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence violations. The assessed civil money penalty is $350 million.

Additionally, the OCC imposed a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., Charlotte, North Carolina, for similar deficiencies in its BSA/AML compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. This is the largest civil money penalty in OCC history.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Prohibition Orders Against Former Bank Employees for Embezzlement
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has issued Orders of Prohibition against two former bank employees for embezzling customer funds. These actions underscore the OCC's commitment to holding individuals accountable for their conduct within financial institutions.
Jennifer Hamblin, a Vault Teller at a Cincinnati, Ohio, branch of Fifth Third Bank, N.A., Cincinnati, Ohio, was prohibited for embezzling approximately $292,000 in customer funds.

Similarly, Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at the La Mirada, California Operations Center of U.S. Bank National Association, Cincinnati, Ohio, received a prohibition order for embezzling approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
